title: Walter Kohn, a child refugee from Vienna, developed density functional theory and won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry

paragraphs.text: Walter Kohn was born on 9 March 1923 in Vienna.
His Jewish parents were Salomon and Gittel Kohn.
According to the National Academy of Sciences biographical memoir, it was an educated, middle-class Jewish family.
According to The Canadian Encyclopedia, his father ran a publishing company that produced artistic postcards.
According to The Canadian Encyclopedia, soon after the annexation of Austria by Nazi Germany in March 1938, Kohn was expelled from the Akademisches Gymnasium.
According to Physics Today, he was admitted to a Jewish gymnasium, where two remarkable teachers awoke his interest in science.
According to The Canadian Encyclopedia, on the day after Kristallnacht the family home was broken into, and Walter was arrested on his way home from school and later released.
According to the University of California, Santa Barbara, the Kindertransport saved Walter and his sister Minna, together with some 10,000 other children, most of them Jewish.
According to ChemistryViews, he lived in Britain with a foster family in Sussex.
According to The Canadian Encyclopedia, his parents were unable to escape and were later murdered at Auschwitz.
According to the National Academy of Sciences biographical memoir, in May 1940 Kohn was interned as an enemy alien, together with tens of thousands of foreign residents in England.
According to The Canadian Encyclopedia, he was held for a year and a half in four internment camps in New Brunswick and Quebec.
According to the Academy, a school that operated in the camp allowed him to continue studying physics and mathematics.
According to The Canadian Encyclopedia, he bought a mathematics and physics textbook with the wages he earned from cutting trees.
According to the Academy, Hertha and Bruno Mendel invited him and his friend Josef Eisinger to live with them in Toronto.
According to The Canadian Encyclopedia, he was released from Camp N into the care of the Mendel family.

According to the National Academy of Sciences memoir, Kohn's life changed decisively in the fall of 1941, and according to The Canadian Encyclopedia, he was released from Camp N into the care of the Mendel family in Toronto in January 1942.

stations.title: From Toronto to Harvard and the solid state

paragraphs.text: According to the Academy, Leopold Infeld advised him to study in the Math-Physics program in Toronto.
According to The Canadian Encyclopedia, the dean of the faculty gave him a special dispensation that removed chemistry from the program's requirements.
By his own account, after several attempts he was accepted into the Canadian Infantry Corps in the last year of World War II.
According to the University of Toronto, in 1945 he completed a bachelor's degree in mathematics and physics.
In 1946 he moved to Harvard, where Julian Schwinger was his doctoral adviser.
In just two years he completed a doctorate on the quantum mechanical description of collisions between light nuclei.
His early work was in theoretical mechanics and quantum field theory, and he soon turned to solid-state theory.

According to the National Academy of Sciences memoir, Carnegie Tech offered him a post starting in the fall of 1950, but he delayed the move to Pittsburgh and in January 1951 took his family to the Niels Bohr Institute in Copenhagen, staying until the summer of 1952.
According to the Academy, in the fall of 1952 he returned to the United States, to Carnegie Tech, and there played a central role in building a strong research program in solid state physics.
At Carnegie Tech he developed a theory of anomalies in the phonon spectra of metals, now known as Kohn anomalies.
According to The Canadian Encyclopedia, he was a consultant at Bell Laboratories in New Jersey and returned there each summer for over a decade.
In 1960 he moved to the new campus of the University of California, San Diego, and headed the physics department in its early period.
In 1961 he received the Oliver E. Buckley Prize of the American Physical Society.

stations.title: The idea: density instead of wave functions

paragraphs.text: According to the Nobel Foundation, quantum mechanics requires very complicated calculations for complex systems such as molecules.
According to the Academy, a great deal of effort was spent extending perturbation methods to many-body problems, where the interactions are strong and perturbative approximations are problematic.
According to Hohenberg, he met Kohn in 1963, when he was a postdoc in Paris, and Kohn invited him to join a new research project.
In their first paper, from 1964, the two presented an exact, variational reformulation of many-body quantum theory.
In place of the wave functions it used a single electron density, dependent on position.
In the words of the Nobel Foundation, one could look at the average density of electrons in space instead of following the motion of each electron.
The result applies to arbitrarily large numbers of electrons, in any arrangement of atomic nuclei.
It applies equally well to chemical molecules of any complexity.
Kohn and Lu Sham recast the theory as an exact set of generalized Hartree-Fock equations, all expressed in terms of the electron density.
The method gives useful approximate solutions with no more difficulty than the conventional Hartree-Fock method, but with significantly better accuracy.
Only with the advent of fast, powerful computers did density functional theory become the method of choice for research in materials physics and chemistry.
Since the 1980s chemists have used it to predict the properties of complex atoms and molecules.
According to the Royal Society, the approach greatly simplified the computations needed to understand the electron bonding between atoms within molecules.
According to The Canadian Encyclopedia, it became useful in physics, chemistry, biochemistry, materials science and engineering.
In 2005 Redner listed the Hohenberg-Kohn and Kohn-Sham papers as the most cited publications in the history of the journal Physical Review.
According to Hohenberg, the joint paper by him and Kohn is the second most cited there.
In 1998 Kohn won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry, together with John Pople.
He received half of the prize, for the development of density functional theory.
According to ChemistryViews, the prize was awarded to both for their contributions to the understanding of the electronic properties of materials.
According to the Academy, the prize was awarded about thirty years after the discovery, once its importance had become clear.
According to Hohenberg, the paper they wrote in the spring of 1964 was one of two works cited by the Nobel Committee in awarding the prize.
According to the University of Toronto, Kohn was one of five Nobel laureates who studied there.
According to the University of California, Santa Barbara, he was the first of its six Nobel laureates since 1998.

stations.title: Santa Barbara, Judaism and the sun

paragraphs.text: According to Physics Today, Kohn was recruited by the University of California, Santa Barbara, as founding director of the Institute for Theoretical Physics.

According to the university, it was he who essentially launched the institute, and the institute quickly developed into one of the leading research centers in physics and has been emulated around the world.
According to the Academy, the institute soon became a destination of choice for scientists from around the world.
According to Jim Langer, the university's rise to an internationally prominent research university was due in large part to the institute's reputation.
Today the institute is housed in Kohn Hall, a building that bears his name.
In the autobiography he wrote for the Nobel Foundation, Kohn wrote that he has a strong Jewish identity.
According to the University of Toronto, he established a program in Judaic Studies at the University of California, San Diego.
In 1978 he remarried, to Mara Vishniac, the daughter of the photographer Roman Vishniac and, like him, a Jewish refugee from Nazi persecution.
He was active in the scientific community in defending the human rights of scientists worldwide.
According to the University of Toronto, he campaigned against the nuclear arms race.
In 2001 he was the inaugural speaker for the Templeton Lectures on Science, Religion, and the Human Experience.
According to the Royal Society, in 2005 he co-produced an educational film on solar energy, narrated by John Cleese.
In May 2009 he gave a lecture at Bar-Ilan University, on receiving an honorary doctorate from it.
Kohn died at his home in Santa Barbara on 19 April 2016.
Physics Today: in 1979, as founding director of the Institute for Theoretical Physics

stations.title: A struggle that did not succeed

paragraphs.text: Kohn was a leader of a faculty effort to sever the link between the University of California and the nuclear weapons laboratories at Los Alamos and Livermore.
According to Physics Today, this effort has so far been unsuccessful.

claims.text: וולטר קוהן קיבל מחצית מפרס נובל בכימיה על פיתוח תורת פונקציונל הצפיפות.
claims.quote: Half of prize for his development of the density-functional theory

claims.text: לפי ChemistryViews, פרס נובל הוענק לקוהן ולפופל על תרומתם להבנת התכונות האלקטרוניות של חומרים.
claims.quote: contributions to the understandings of the electronic properties of materials

claims.text: לפי ההספד של האקדמיה הלאומית למדעים, כשלושים שנה אחרי הגילוי, לאחר שחשיבותו התבהרה, הוענק לקוהן פרס נובל בכימיה.
claims.quote: Thirty years later, once the vast importance of this theory had become clear, he was awarded a Nobel Prize in Chemistry for this discovery.

claims.text: לפי הוהנברג, המאמר שפרסמו באביב 1964 היה אחת משתי עבודות שוועדת נובל ציינה בהענקת הפרס.
claims.quote: was one of two works cited by the Nobel Committee in awarding the 1998 Chemistry Prize to Walter

claims.text: לפי אוניברסיטת טורונטו, קוהן היה אחד מחמישה זוכי נובל שלמדו באוניברסיטה.
claims.quote: One of five Nobel laureates to have graduated from U of T

claims.text: לפי אוניברסיטת קליפורניה בסנטה ברברה, קוהן היה הראשון מבין שישה זוכי נובל של האוניברסיטה מאז 1998.
claims.quote: the first of six Nobel laureates at UC Santa Barbara since 1998

claims.text: לפי אוניברסיטת קליפורניה בסנטה ברברה, המכון לפיזיקה תאורטית הושק למעשה על ידי קוהן.
claims.quote: the Institute for Theoretical Physics (ITP), as it was then known, was essentially launched by Kohn

claims.text: לפי אוניברסיטת קליפורניה בסנטה ברברה, המכון התפתח במהירות לאחד ממרכזי המחקר המובילים בפיזיקה ומוּדל בעולם.
claims.quote: quickly developed into one of the leading research centers in physics, and has since been widely emulated internationally

claims.text: לפי ההספד של האקדמיה הלאומית למדעים, המכון הפך במהרה ליעד מועדף על מדענים מכל העולם.
claims.quote: the ITP quickly became a destination of choice for scientists throughout the world

claims.text: לפי ג'ים לנגר, עלייתה של אוניברסיטת סנטה ברברה לאוניברסיטת מחקר בולטת בעולם נבעה במידה רבה ממוניטין המכון.
claims.quote: The rise of UCSB as an internationally prominent research university was due in large part to the growing reputation of the ITP.

claims.text: המכון שוכן כיום בבניין בשם Kohn Hall, הנושא את שמו של קוהן.
claims.quote: Now situated in a building, Kohn Hall, that bears his name

claims.text: קוהן אמר בנאום הנובל שלו שיש לו זהות יהודית חזקה.
claims.quote: I want to mention that I have a strong Jewish identity

claims.text: לפי אוניברסיטת טורונטו, קוהן פעל נגד מרוץ החימוש הגרעיני, הפיק סרט תיעודי על אנרגיית שמש והקים תוכנית ללימודי יהדות באוניברסיטת קליפורניה בסן דייגו.
claims.quote: He campaigned against the nuclear arms race, produced a documentary on solar power and established a program in Judaic Studies at the University of California, San Diego.

claims.text: ב-1978 נישא קוהן בשנית למארה וישניאק, בתו של הצלם רומן וישניאק ופליטה יהודייה מרדיפות הנאצים כמוהו.
claims.quote: Walter was remarried in 1978, to Mara Vishniac, the daughter of the photographer Roman Vishniac and, like Walter, a Jewish refugee from Nazi oppression.

claims.text: קוהן פעל בקהילה המדעית להגנה על זכויות האדם של מדענים ברחבי העולם.
claims.quote: He was active in efforts in the scientific community to defend the human rights of scientists worldwide.

claims.text: ב-2001 היה קוהן הדובר הראשון בהרצאות טמפלטון על מדע, דת וחוויית האדם.
claims.quote: In 2001, he was the inaugural speaker for the Templeton Research Lectures on Science, Religion, and the Human Experience

claims.text: לפי החברה המלכותית, ב-2005 הפיק קוהן יחד עם אחרים סרט לימודי על אנרגיית השמש בהקראת ג'ון קליס.
claims.quote: a classroom documentary on solar power narrated by John Cleese

claims.text: קוהן מת בביתו בסנטה ברברה, קליפורניה, ב-19 באפריל 2016.
claims.quote: Walter Kohn, a giant of 20th-century theoretical physics, died at his home in Santa Barbara, California, on 19 April 2016.

claims.text: קוהן היה מנהיג של מאמץ סגל לנתק את הקשר בין אוניברסיטת קליפורניה למעבדות הנשק הגרעיני בלוס אלמוס ובליברמור, מאמץ שעד כה לא צלח.
claims.quote: He was a leader of the (so far unsuccessful) faculty effort to sever the link between the University of California and the US nuclear weapons laboratories at Los Alamos and Livermore.

claims.text: הוריו היהודים היו סלומון וגיטל קוהן.
claims.quote: He was born as Walter Samuel Gerst Kohn on March 9, 1923, in Vienna, Austria, to Salomon and Gittel Kohn.

claims.text: במאי 2009 נשא הרצאה באוניברסיטת בר-אילן, כשקיבל ממנה תואר דוקטור לשם כבוד.
claims.quote: receiving an honorary doctorate in Bar-Ilan in May 2009

claims.text: לפי ההספד של האקדמיה הלאומית למדעים, קרנגי טק הציע לו משרה מסתיו 1950, אבל הוא דחה את המעבר לפיטסבורג ובינואר 1951 נסע עם משפחתו למכון נילס בוהר בקופנהגן, ונשאר שם עד קיץ 1952.
claims.quote: Institute for Theoretical Physics in Copenhagen in January 1951
